Handout: AI Basics for Absolute Beginners

Take this home. It has everything from the first half of class — no jargon, no homework, nothing to sign up for.

The one-paragraph version

AI chat tools are very good guessers of the next word. They learned from a huge pile of reading what answers usually look like. That makes them great for drafts, plans, and explanations — and it means they can sound confident while being wrong. You stay in charge: you review what it says, and you double-check anything important.

What AI chat tools are good at

  • Drafting — emails, thank-you notes, social posts, short letters.
  • Planning — meals, trips, routines, gift lists, party checklists.
  • Explaining — a plain-English summary of a topic you’re curious about.
  • Simplifying — rewriting something stuffy in everyday words.
  • Ideas — brainstorming when your own well is temporarily dry.

What they are NOT for

  • Medical decisions — they are not a doctor. Take questions to a real clinician.
  • Legal or money decisions — they are not a lawyer or your bank. Not even close.
  • Anything requiring your private info — more on that in the safety handout.
  • Emotional crises — no chat can replace a person who loves you, or 988.

The 3-step prompt recipe

Think: role → context → ask.

  1. Role — give it a job title. “You are a patient librarian.”
  2. Context — the details that matter. “Cooking for two, mild spice.”
  3. Ask — say exactly what you want back. “Give me a 5-dinner plan as a list.”

Five ready-made prompt recipes

  1. The planner: “You are a friendly local guide. Plan one relaxed afternoon exploring a mid-size U.S. downtown on a budget, for someone who walks slowly and likes local history. Give me 3 stops and a rough time for each.”
  2. The writer: “You are my polite editor. Draft a friendly 100-word thank-you note to the volunteers who helped at the library book sale. Keep it warm, not sappy.”
  3. The simplifier: “You are a patient explainer for a total beginner. Describe what a ‘cloud backup’ is using a household analogy I’d remember. Two paragraphs, no jargon.”
  4. The nudge: “You are a gentle coach. I keep postponing a 30-minute weekly tidy-up of my files plus one errand I’ve been avoiding. Build me a 3-step plan for this city weekend that starts so small I’d laugh at it.”
  5. The checker: “You are a helpful neighbor. Here’s a phrase I want to say at my neighborhood association meeting: [text]. Tell me in 3 bullet points how it could sound clearer without changing the meaning.”

Ground rules you’ll love

  • No magic words needed. Talk to it like a nice new coworker.
  • The first answer is a draft. Say what’s off and ask again; use its “try again” button without guilt.
  • It doesn’t judge. Ask the question you’ve been embarrassed to ask a person.
  • It doesn’t remember who you are across separate chats in the same way a friend might — brand-new chat, clean slate. Some tools remember within a conversation; that’s the whole memory you get.
  • If a fact really matters — a name, a number, a date, an address — peek at an official source, not just the chat’s word for it.

Plain-English glossary

WordWhat it actually means
AI (artificial intelligence)A family of computer techniques where software performs tasks that used to require human judgments — like understanding text or recognizing a photo. Today’s everyday AI is pattern-matching on steroids, not a thinking mind.
ChatbotA tool where you type to it and it types back. Like texting, except it never needs dinner.
PromptThe thing you type to it. Your half of the conversation. Better prompts = better results, guaranteed.
Large language model (LLM)The pattern-matching engine inside modern chatbots. It predicts the next word from the pattern of everything it has read.
HallucinationTech people’s word for “made something up.” The chat writes a confident answer that simply isn’t true. Best defense: check important facts at the source.
RegenerateThe “roll the dice again” button. A fresh answer without changing your prompt.
